title: The Spreading of Disorder
text:
The broken windows theory holds that visible signs of disorder encourage further disorder and crime. In 2008, Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg and Linda Steg of the University of Groningen in the Netherlands tested this with a series of field experiments on the streets of their city.

In one, they hung flyers on the handlebars of bicycles parked in an alley next to a sign forbidding graffiti. When the wall was clean, about a third of cyclists threw the flyer on the ground. When the wall was covered in graffiti, more than two thirds did.

In another, they left an envelope hanging out of a mailbox, with a five-euro note clearly visible inside. When the mailbox was clean and the area tidy, about 13 percent of passersby took the envelope. When the mailbox was covered in graffiti, the share rose to 27 percent, and litter around it had a similar effect.

Other experiments showed similar patterns with fences, shopping carts and fireworks. Seeing that others had broken one rule made people more likely to break different rules. The authors argued that visible violations weaken people's sense that norms in general apply.
lesson: Small visible lapses in a shared space signal that rules no longer matter. Fix minor disorder quickly so it does not spread to bigger things.
people: Kees Keizer, Siegwart Lindenberg, Linda Steg
source: Keizer, K., Lindenberg, S., and Steg, L. (2008). The spreading of disorder. Science, 322(5908), 1681-1685.
